description: How al-Mansour and Sciamma represent young women navigating constraint, agency and identity.
content_html:
Two Films, Two Constrained Worlds

Wadjda (Haifaa Al-Mansour, 2012) and Girlhood (Céline Sciamma, 2014) share a central representational project: showing young women navigating worlds in which their freedom of movement, self-expression and identity are constrained by gender, culture and economic circumstance. Both films use specific filmic choices to represent their protagonists as subjects with agency rather than passive objects of social pressure. Understanding how each film constructs agency through framing, camera placement, music and editing is the core analytical task for this lesson.

Key Fact

Wadjda (2012): directed by Haifaa Al-Mansour; shot in Riyadh; cinematographer Lutz Reitemeier; score by Max Richter; made for approximately three million euros. Girlhood (2014): directed by Céline Sciamma; shot in the Paris suburbs; cinematographer Crystel Fournier; score by Para One. Both films were made by women directors, which is a significant AO1 context for their representation of young women.

Framing as Enclosure: Wadjda

Al-Mansour’s most consistently used formal strategy is framing female characters through doorways, windows and corridors — architectural features that function as visual metaphors for the social restrictions placed on women and girls in the film’s setting. In the film’s early sequences, Wadjda’s mother is frequently seen at the threshold of rooms rather than at their centre: standing in doorways, looking out through window grilles, positioned at the edges of frames. The frame-within-a-frame composition makes enclosure visible. But Al-Mansour reserves a different visual treatment for Wadjda herself: the ten-year-old is often filmed in open space — the school corridor, the street — with room to move in the frame. Her low-angle shot perspective, frequently adopted when the camera takes Wadjda’s point of view, gives her visual authority over the spaces she occupies.

Named Sequence: The Toy-Shop Bicycle Reveal

In the toy-shop bicycle reveal, Wadjda first sees the green bicycle that becomes the film’s central symbol. Al-Mansour cuts from a medium shot of Wadjda walking past the shop to a point-of-view shot through the shop window: the bicycle sits on a display stand, lit by the warm overhead shop lighting, a rack-focus pulling it from blur to crisp sharpness as Wadjda’s gaze settles. The bicycle is introduced visually before it is named by any character. This is a precise micro choice: the spectator receives the visual information through Wadjda’s looking — her subjectivity governs what we see and when we see it. The bicycle is not a scenic prop. It is the object of Wadjda’s desire, and the point-of-view shot makes that desire ours too. The macro meaning is clear: Al-Mansour represents Wadjda as a seeing, desiring subject, not an object of observation.

The bicycle in Wadjda is a visual object that carries representational weight beyond its function as a toy. Bicycles give children physical mobility — the ability to go further, faster, beyond the immediate neighbourhood. In the film’s setting, girls are not supposed to ride bicycles in public spaces. When Wadjda pursues and eventually obtains the bicycle, the closing street-traversal sequence — in which she rides it freely through the neighbourhood while Abdullah races alongside her — represents more than a child getting what she wanted. The open space of the street and the physical freedom of movement stand against the indoor, threshold-framed enclosure of the film’s earlier sequences. The camera follows rather than leads her: it does not know where she is going, and neither do we. This is the representational argument of the film’s ending: agency is not just desired but enacted.

Named Sequence: The Hotel-Room Karaoke Set Piece in Girlhood

In the hotel-room karaoke set piece, Marieme and her three new friends rent a hotel room for the night and perform Rihanna’s “Diamonds” together in blue-gelled light. Cinematographer Crystel Fournier frames the four girls in a wide Cinemascope shot: they fill the horizontal width of the frame together, their bodies in motion, the blue light making the scene feel removed from the grey social realism of the film’s exterior sequences. This is a sustained set piece — it runs for several minutes without a cut to any outside observer. There is no adult authority figure in the room. There is no male gaze directing the spectator’s attention: the camera is at the friends’ own level, and when it moves it follows their movement rather than surveilling them. Laura Mulvey’s gaze theory is useful here at GCSE level: who is looking at whom in this frame? The answer is that the four girls are looking at themselves and each other. The gaze is internal to the group. The spectator is invited into a space of female self-creation, not into a position of surveillance over it.

A common error in answering representation questions about these two films is to assume that films about young women automatically empower them. Representation analysis asks how the film constructs its subjects through specific filmic choices, not just whether it has a female protagonist. Girlhood has also generated critical debate about whether a white French director (Sciamma) making a film about Black teenage girls in the banlieues carries an inherent representational tension, regardless of the film’s formal choices. At GCSE level, it is appropriate to note this cultural-ethics question as part of the film’s reception context (AO1), while focusing your analysis on the specific filmic choices and their effects on representation (AO2). The question is not whether the film is “good” representation, but how it constructs representation through the tools of cinema.

Costume and Music as Identity

Both films use costume and music as identity-construction tools. In Girlhood, the saturated colour of the friends’ clothing — vivid blues, pinks and purples worn in contrast to the greys and browns of the suburban exterior — functions as a colour code for identity: the girls’ brightness is an assertion of presence in a landscape that otherwise renders them invisible. Para One’s score uses extended needle-drops (sustained songs played at length rather than as background) to give the friends’ interior scenes an anthem quality. In Wadjda, the green trainers Wadjda customises with painted stars are a micro-detail of non-conformity: they sit beneath the uniform abaya she is required to wear, visible only to her and to the spectator. The film frames these trainers in close-up twice — a deliberate editorial choice to give weight to a small act of self-expression.

Key Fact

The hotel-room karaoke set piece in Girlhood is one of the most analysed sequences in recent European cinema. Its representational power comes from three micro choices working together: Cinemascope widescreen framing placing all four girls as equal subjects in the frame; blue-gel lighting separating the scene from social-realist exteriors; and the absence of any external observer, male or adult. The gaze belongs to the girls themselves.
exam_tip_html: For a micro-analysis question on either Wadjda or Girlhood, stay inside one short named sequence and unpack it through at least three distinct micro features. The most common error is spreading the answer across the whole film (“throughout the film, Wadjda is shown as determined”) rather than analysing how a specific moment constructs that representation. For each micro feature — a low-angle shot, a point-of-view cut, a colour choice, a music cue — state what it is, then say what it does: what representation does it construct and what effect does it have on the spectator’s relationship to the character? For extended-essay questions, the gaze theory (Mulvey) is a useful framework but must be applied to a specific shot rather than mentioned in the abstract. Your thesis should make a claim about what the film argues through its representation, not just describe what the film contains.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Wadjda uses frame-within-a-frame compositions for female characters in constrained spaces, while reserving point-of-view low-angle shots for Wadjda herself — constructing her as a seeing, desiring subject rather than an object of observation.
  • The hotel-room karaoke set piece in Girlhood places the gaze inside the group of friends through Cinemascope framing, blue-gel lighting and the absence of external observers — representing Black femininity as a space of self-creation, not surveillance.
  • Costume and music function as identity codes in both films: Girlhood’s saturated colours assert presence; Wadjda’s customised trainers are a close-up detail of private non-conformity beneath visible restriction.

practice_questions.text: Identify the name of the cinematographer on Girlhood (2014).
What is meant by the term 'frame-within-a-frame' as a compositional technique?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining the technique as one where the main subject is seen through another frame inside the shot, such as a doorway, window or archway; 1 mark for explaining its representational effect (e.g. it directs the spectator's attention and adds visual meaning, often used to suggest enclosure or restriction in Wadjda).

practice_questions.text: Explain how Haifaa Al-Mansour uses point-of-view cinematography in the toy-shop bicycle reveal sequence of Wadjda to represent Wadjda's agency. Refer to specific camera choices.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for identifying the point-of-view shot through the shop window; 1 mark for naming a specific camera choice (e.g. rack-focus pulling the bicycle from blur to sharpness as Wadjda’s gaze settles; the shot is taken from Wadjda’s eye level); 1 mark for explaining the effect on spectator positioning (e.g. the spectator receives the visual information through Wadjda’s looking — her subjectivity governs what we see and when); 1 mark for linking to the representation of agency (e.g. the bicycle is introduced as the object of Wadjda’s desire, and the point-of-view shot makes it the spectator’s desire too — constructing Wadjda as a seeing subject, not an object of observation); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (point-of-view, rack-focus, spectator positioning, representation, agency).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Crystel Fournier's cinematography in the hotel-room karaoke set piece of Girlhood positions the spectator in relation to Marieme and her friends. Refer to at least three distinct micro-features from the sequence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Answer stays inside the hotel-room karaoke set piece and unpacks at least three distinct micro-features (e.g. Cinemascope widescreen framing placing all four friends as equal subjects in the horizontal frame; blue-gel lighting separating the scene from the grey social realism of exterior sequences; camera at the girls’ own level rather than surveilling from above; the sustained duration of the set piece without cutting to any external observer; the absence of male gaze — the only looking in the frame is the friends looking at themselves and each other). Each feature is linked to a precise representational effect (e.g. the widescreen framing makes the friends’ collective presence the visual event; the internal gaze constructs a space of female self-creation). Macro representation is stated (Black femininity as a space of belonging and collective identity; the film’s challenge to the stereotype of alienated, surveilled banlieue youth). Specialist vocabulary precise throughout.

Secure: Three features identified with mostly accurate effects; named sequence clearly referenced; macro representation present; mostly accurate vocabulary.

Developing: One or two features; effect on spectator implied but not stated; may drift toward describing what happens; limited vocabulary.

Emerging: Generic description without specific micro-features; representation discussed as theme not construction; no spectator positioning discussed.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how either Wadjda or Girlhood uses specific filmic choices to construct a counter-type representation of young women. Refer to at least two named sequences and apply a relevant film theory to your analysis. Reach a justified evaluative judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained thesis argues a specific representational claim (e.g. Wadjda constructs its protagonist as a counter-type by consistently giving her the film’s point-of-view shots, reserving visual agency for the child that the adult women in the film are denied; or Girlhood challenges the surveillance of the banlieue by constructing the karaoke set piece as a space where the gaze belongs to the girls themselves). At least two named sequences analysed with concrete micro-features (e.g. Wadjda: toy-shop bicycle reveal — point-of-view rack-focus; closing street-traversal — following camera coding freedom; Girlhood: hotel-room karaoke — widescreen framing, blue light, internal gaze; opening American-football tracking shot — camera following girls not game). Gaze theory applied to a specific shot (Mulvey: who holds the gaze in the hotel-room sequence). Macro representation sustained throughout. Specialist vocabulary precise. Evaluative judgement is justified with reference to specific sequences.

Secure: Thesis present; two sequences referenced; micro-features identified; theory applied; judgement reached.

Developing: Relevant points but thematic rather than filmic analysis; limited named sequences; limited specialist vocabulary; weak judgement.

Emerging: Plot summary; no thesis; no micro-features; representation described not analysed.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Celine Sciamma uses costume and music as identity codes in Girlhood. Refer to at least two specific moments.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 5 marks: 1 mark for identifying a specific costume choice (e.g. saturated blue, pink and purple clothing worn by the friends in contrast to the grey suburban exterior); 1 mark for explaining its representational effect (e.g. the bright colours function as a visual assertion of presence in a landscape that otherwise renders the girls invisible); 1 mark for identifying a specific music choice (e.g. Para One’s extended needle-drop — a full song sustained at length rather than as background music — in the hotel-room karaoke sequence); 1 mark for explaining its effect (e.g. the anthem-like quality of the sustained song gives the friends’ interior scenes an emotional scale that contrasts with the muted sound design of exterior sequences); 1 mark for accurate specialist vocabulary (mise-en-scene, colour code, non-diegetic, diegetic, needle-drop, spectator positioning).

knowledge_checks.q: In Wadjda, what object does the protagonist save up to buy, and what does it represent in the film?
options: A school uniform, representing academic achievement
A mobile phone, representing modern communication
A green bicycle, representing mobility and agency
A music player, representing personal freedom

knowledge_checks.q: In the hotel-room karaoke set piece in Girlhood, whose gaze governs the sequence?
options: The teacher who arrives at the hotel
The four friends looking at themselves and each other
The camera operator filming from outside the room

knowledge_checks.q: Al-Mansour frequently films female characters in Wadjda through doorways and windows, a compositional technique called _____ within a frame.
In Girlhood, Crystel Fournier uses _____ widescreen framing to place all four friends as equal subjects across the horizontal width of the frame.
Match each micro choice to its representational effect in these two films:
left: Blue-gel lighting in the hotel room (Girlhood)
right: Constructs Wadjda as a seeing, desiring subject with visual agency
Separates the scene from social-realist exterior sequences, creating a space of female self-creation
Gives weight to a small private act of non-conformity beneath visible restriction

flashcard_questions.a: Framing the main subject through a doorway, window or arch inside the shot, adding visual meaning.
A shot taken from below, looking upward, making the subject appear larger or more powerful.

flashcard_questions.q: What is agency as a representational concept in film?
flashcard_questions.a: The ability of a character to act independently and make choices, as constructed through filmic choices.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a colour code in film mise-en-scene?
flashcard_questions.a: A visual code where costume, set or lighting colours signal character emotion, status or theme.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the production context for Wadjda's director Haifaa Al-Mansour?
flashcard_questions.a: She directed many street scenes from inside a van, as women directing men in public was restricted in Saudi Arabia at the time.

flashcard_questions.q: Who won the Carrosse d'Or at Cannes Directors' Fortnight 2014?
What is a needle-drop in film sound design?
flashcard_questions.a: A pre-existing song played at sustained length in a scene rather than as brief background music.

flashcard_questions.q: Apply Mulvey's gaze theory to the hotel-room karaoke set piece in Girlhood — who holds the gaze?
flashcard_questions.a: The four friends look at themselves and each other — the gaze is internal to the group, not external.
A shot that shows what a character is looking at, placing the spectator inside the character's perspective.
A camera technique where focus shifts from one subject to another within a single shot.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the bicycle symbolise in Wadjda?
flashcard_questions.a: Physical mobility and agency — freedom of movement for a girl in a restricted social world.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the score composer for Girlhood?

glossary_terms.definition: The ability or power of an individual to act independently, make choices, and influence their own circumstances, as represented through filmic choices.

A compositional technique in which the main subject is seen through or within another frame inside the shot, such as a doorway, window or archway, directing the spectator's attention and adding visual meaning.
A shot taken from a camera position close to the ground, looking upward, which typically makes the subject appear larger, more powerful or more significant.
A visual code in film in which the colours of costumes, set design and lighting signal character emotion, social status or thematic meaning without dialogue.
A shot that shows what a character is looking at from their perspective, placing the spectator inside the character's subjectivity.
A widescreen cinematographic format with an aspect ratio of approximately 2.35:1, which produces a wide horizontal frame often used to compose ensemble or landscape shots.
A critical framework associated with Laura Mulvey arguing that mainstream cinema has historically constructed women as objects to be looked at rather than as subjects who look.
